questions.fact: Pitchers were so strong that year that baseball lowered the pitcher's mound for 1969.

questions.question: Which injured Knicks captain limped onto the court to inspire New York in Game 7 of the 1970 NBA Finals?
questions.fact: He scored the team's first two baskets, and the Knicks won their first championship.

questions.question: Secretariat won the 1973 Belmont Stakes by how many lengths?
questions.fact: His time of 2 minutes 24 seconds is still the Belmont Stakes record.

questions.question: Who beat Muhammad Ali in their 1971 'Fight of the Century'?
questions.fact: It was Ali's first loss as a professional. Frank Sinatra took photos at ringside for Life magazine.

questions.question: Who coached the 1972 Miami Dolphins, the only NFL team to finish a whole season unbeaten?
questions.fact: They went 17-0, finishing with a win over Washington in Super Bowl VII.

questions.question: The Buffalo Bills won their second straight AFL title in 1965. Which team did they beat?
questions.fact: They beat the same team in the 1964 title game, too.

questions.question: Which Orioles relief pitcher struck out 11 Dodgers in Game 1 of the 1966 World Series?
questions.fact: Baltimore swept the Dodgers in four games.

questions.question: England won the 1966 World Cup. Who scored three goals in the final?
questions.fact: England beat West Germany 4 to 2 at Wembley Stadium in London.

questions.question: In the 1966 college basketball final, Texas Western started five Black players and beat which famous team?
questions.fact: Coach Don Haskins's Miners beat Adolph Rupp's Kentucky Wildcats. The game is now seen as a turning point for the sport.

questions.question: Which pitcher led the Boston Red Sox in their 1967 'Impossible Dream' season?
questions.fact: He won 22 games and the Cy Young Award.

questions.question: Which Orioles third baseman's fielding in the 1970 World Series earned him the nickname 'the Human Vacuum Cleaner'?
questions.fact: He won 16 Gold Gloves in a row and was named MVP of that World Series.

questions.question: Which Pirates star was named MVP of the 1971 World Series?
questions.fact: He collected his 3,000th hit in his last regular-season game, in September 1972.

questions.question: Which showman owner of the Oakland A's paid his players to grow mustaches in 1972?
questions.fact: His team mascot was a mule named Charlie O, and the A's won three World Series in a row.

questions.question: Which Miami Dolphins fullback was named MVP of Super Bowl VIII in January 1974?
questions.fact: He ran for 145 yards and two touchdowns against the Minnesota Vikings.

questions.question: What made Houston's Astrodome, opened in 1965, so new and different?
options: It had a roof over the whole field
questions.fact: It was called 'the Eighth Wonder of the World.' Real grass would not grow inside, which led to AstroTurf.

questions.question: Peggy Fleming won America's only gold medal at the 1968 Winter Olympics. In which sport?
questions.fact: She skated in a chartreuse dress that her mother had sewn for her.

questions.question: In 1969, which once-hopeless team shocked baseball by winning the World Series?
questions.fact: They became known as the 'Miracle Mets' after beating the Baltimore Orioles.

questions.question: In 1972, American Bobby Fischer became world champion of which game?
questions.fact: He beat Boris Spassky of the Soviet Union in Reykjavík, Iceland.

questions.question: Which tiny Soviet gymnast charmed TV viewers around the world at the 1972 Olympics?
questions.fact: She was 17 and won three gold medals. Her daring backflips made gymnastics hugely popular.

questions.question: What was the name of the backward high-jump style that won Olympic gold in 1968?
questions.fact: Dick Fosbury went over the bar head first and on his back. Almost every high jumper uses it today.

questions.question: Which Boston Bruins defenseman was photographed flying through the air after his Cup-winning goal in 1970?
questions.fact: The goal won the Stanley Cup in overtime. The famous photo is now a statue outside Boston's arena.

questions.question: Which country hosted the 1968 Summer Olympics?
questions.fact: They were the first Olympics held in Latin America. Mexico City's high altitude helped many runners and jumpers set records.

questions.question: Who won the first U.S. Open tennis tournament of the open era, in 1968?
questions.fact: He was still an amateur and an Army lieutenant at the time, so he couldn't accept the prize money.

questions.question: Whose silhouette is said to be the model for the NBA's logo, designed in 1969?
questions.fact: He played for the Los Angeles Lakers and was nicknamed 'Mr. Clutch.'

questions.question: In 1971, astronaut Alan Shepard became the first person to play which sport on the Moon?
questions.fact: He hit two golf balls with a club head attached to a tool handle, and joked that one went 'miles and miles.'

questions.question: In 1973, the American League added a player who bats instead of the pitcher. What is he called?
questions.fact: Ron Blomberg of the Yankees was the first designated hitter to come to bat.

questions.question: Which Steelers running back made the 'Immaculate Reception' in a 1972 playoff game?
questions.fact: He scooped up a deflected pass just before it hit the ground and ran it in for the winning touchdown.

questions.question: Which Red Sox slugger, nicknamed 'Yaz,' won baseball's Triple Crown in 1967?
questions.fact: Fans called him 'Yaz.' No American League player won the Triple Crown again until 2012.

questions.question: Which center, then known as Lew Alcindor, led the Milwaukee Bucks to the 1971 NBA title?
questions.fact: He took the name Kareem Abdul-Jabbar later in 1971 and became famous for his 'skyhook' shot.

questions.question: Which engaged couple both won the Wimbledon singles titles in 1974?
questions.fact: Chris Evert and Jimmy Connors were called tennis's 'Lovebird Double.' They never married.

questions.question: In 1966, Bill Russell became the first Black head coach in the NBA. Which team did he coach?
questions.fact: He was still playing at the same time, and led the Celtics to two more titles as player-coach.

questions.question: In 1968, Denny McLain of the Detroit Tigers won how many games, the most in decades?
questions.fact: No major league pitcher has won 30 games in a season since.

questions.question: Which Australian tennis star won all four major titles in 1969, the second time he did it?
questions.fact: He first won the Grand Slam as an amateur in 1962, and again as a pro in 1969.

questions.question: Sandy Koufax threw a perfect game in 1965. Which team did he do it against?
questions.fact: It was the fourth no-hitter of his career, then a major league record.

questions.question: Which teenage runner from Kansas set the world record in the mile in 1966?
questions.fact: He had become the first high school runner to break four minutes in the mile, in 1964.

questions.question: At the 1968 Olympics, Bob Beamon set a stunning world record in which event?
questions.fact: He jumped about 29 feet 2 inches, almost two feet past the old record. It stood for 23 years.

questions.question: In 1970, which player won his third World Cup with Brazil?
questions.fact: He is still the only player to win three World Cups.

questions.question: Which golfer, nicknamed 'Super Mex,' won the US, Canadian and British Opens in 1971?
questions.fact: He won all three within about a month, and was named Sports Illustrated's Sportsman of the Year.

questions.question: Which Detroit pitcher won three games to beat the Cardinals in the 1968 World Series?
questions.fact: He beat Bob Gibson in Game 7 and was named the Series MVP.

questions.question: Who became Major League Baseball's first Black manager when Cleveland hired him in 1974?
questions.fact: He was also a player then, and he hit a home run in his first game as player-manager in 1975.

questions.question: Which American won the marathon at the 1972 Olympics, helping start the running boom?
questions.fact: He was born in Munich, Germany, the very city where he won his gold medal.

questions.question: Finish Neil Armstrong's first words on the Moon: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for…'
questions.fact: He later said he meant to say 'one small step for a man,' and that the 'a' was lost.

questions.question: In 1971, the 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to what?
questions.fact: It was ratified faster than any other amendment, in a little over three months.

questions.question: The 1972 break-in that led to President Nixon's downfall happened at which Washington building complex?
questions.fact: The burglars were caught on June 17, 1972, after a security guard noticed tape on a door lock.

questions.question: Who was the first president of the National Organization for Women, founded in 1966?
questions.fact: She was the author of 'The Feminine Mystique.'

questions.question: The 1967 'Summer of Love' centered on which San Francisco neighborhood?
questions.fact: About 100,000 young people poured in, many wearing flowers in their hair, as the song said.

questions.question: About how many Americans took part in the first Earth Day, on April 22, 1970?
questions.fact: It helped lead to the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency later that year.

questions.question: Congress passed the ERA in 1972. What does ERA stand for?
questions.fact: It said equal rights could not be denied 'on account of sex,' but not enough states approved it in time.

questions.question: Which group of oil-producing nations cut off oil shipments to the US in 1973?
questions.fact: Gas lines stretched around the block, and many stations ran out of fuel.

questions.question: Who replaced Spiro Agnew as vice president when Agnew resigned in 1973?
questions.fact: He was the first vice president chosen under the 25th Amendment, rather than elected.

questions.question: Richard Nixon left office in August 1974. How did his presidency end?
questions.fact: He is the only US president ever to resign. Gerald Ford said, 'Our long national nightmare is over.'

questions.question: Ed White became the first American to walk in space in June 1965. About how long was he outside?
questions.fact: He steered with a hand-held gas gun and did not want to come back in.

questions.question: The 25th Amendment, ratified in 1967, deals with what?
questions.fact: It set rules for replacing a vice president, and for when a president is unable to serve.

questions.question: Who secretly arranged President Nixon's historic 1972 trip to China?
questions.fact: He slipped into China while reporters thought he was resting in Pakistan.

questions.question: Which Ohio river caught fire in 1969, helping lead to the Clean Water Act?
questions.fact: It flows through Cleveland and had caught fire many times before. Time magazine's story made it famous.

questions.question: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module that landed on the Moon in 1969?
questions.fact: Neil Armstrong radioed, 'Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.'

questions.question: Who walked on the Moon with Neil Armstrong in 1969?
questions.fact: Michael Collins circled overhead in the command module, Columbia.

questions.question: How many astronauts flew on the Apollo 11 Moon mission?
questions.fact: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins all came home safely on July 24, 1969.

questions.question: Which health insurance program for older Americans did President Johnson sign into law in 1965?
questions.fact: He signed it in Independence, Missouri, and gave the very first Medicare card to former President Harry Truman.

questions.question: To save fuel, what national highway speed limit was set in 1974?
questions.fact: It stayed the national limit until 1995.

questions.question: Which city's giant stainless steel Gateway Arch was finished in 1965?
questions.fact: At 630 feet, it is the tallest arch in the world. Visitors ride tiny tram cars to the top.

questions.question: Which Hollywood actor was elected governor of California in 1966?
questions.fact: He served two terms and was later elected president, in 1980.

questions.question: Which three-digit emergency phone number was first used in the US in 1968?
questions.fact: The first 9-1-1 call was made in Haleyville, Alabama.

questions.question: Which giant 'jumbo jet' began carrying passengers in January 1970?
questions.fact: Pan Am flew the first one from New York to London. It had a little upstairs lounge.

questions.question: Which Chicago skyscraper, finished in 1973, became the world's tallest building?
questions.fact: It held the title for about 25 years. Today it is called Willis Tower.

questions.question: Which national passenger railroad began running trains in 1971?
questions.fact: It took over most of the country's long-distance passenger trains from private railroads.

questions.question: Two giant pandas arrived at the National Zoo in 1972 as a gift from which country?
questions.fact: Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing were a gift after President Nixon's visit to China.

questions.question: Which famous building with a roof like giant white sails opened in Australia in 1973?
questions.fact: Queen Elizabeth II opened it. A Danish architect, Jørn Utzon, designed it.

questions.question: In 1969, Queen Elizabeth's son Charles was formally crowned Prince of where?
questions.fact: The ceremony was held at Caernarfon Castle and was watched by millions on TV.

questions.question: In 1971, Apollo 15 astronauts became the first to drive what on the Moon?
questions.fact: It was nicknamed the 'moon buggy' and folded up to fit in the lander.

questions.question: Skylab, launched in 1973, was America's first what?
questions.fact: Three crews lived and worked aboard it, the last staying for 84 days.

questions.question: Which Canadian city hosted the 1967 World's Fair, called Expo 67?
questions.fact: It celebrated Canada's 100th birthday, and over 50 million visits were counted.

questions.question: At Christmas 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts took a famous photo of Earth rising over what?
questions.fact: The picture, called 'Earthrise,' was taken by astronaut Bill Anders.

questions.question: In April 1970, the crew of which Apollo mission made it safely home after an explosion on board?
questions.fact: They used the lunar module as a lifeboat. 'Houston, we've had a problem' became a famous line.

questions.question: Who became the first Black justice of the US Supreme Court, in 1967?
questions.fact: As a lawyer, he had won the Brown v. Board of Education case in 1954.

questions.question: Who became vice president after Gerald Ford took over as president in 1974?
questions.fact: He had been governor of New York for 15 years.

questions.question: In 1967, Dr. Christiaan Barnard performed the world's first human heart transplant in which country?
questions.fact: The operation took place at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town.

questions.question: Which supersonic passenger jet, built by Britain and France, made its first flight in 1969?
questions.fact: It could fly from London to New York in about three and a half hours.

questions.question: Which mission, in December 1972, was the last time astronauts walked on the Moon?
questions.fact: Gene Cernan was the last person to step off the Moon.

questions.question: In 1965, Paul VI became the first pope ever to visit which country?
questions.fact: He spoke at the United Nations in New York and said a Mass at Yankee Stadium.

questions.question: Who became India's first woman prime minister in 1966?
questions.fact: She was the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister.

questions.question: Golda Meir became prime minister of which country in 1969?
questions.fact: She had grown up in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and worked there as a schoolteacher.

questions.question: Which British ocean liner, named after a queen, made its first voyage to New York in 1969?
questions.fact: Passengers called her the 'QE2.' She sailed for nearly 40 years.

questions.question: In 1972, which congresswoman became the first Black woman to seek a major party's nomination for president?
questions.fact: Her slogan was 'Unbought and Unbossed.' In 1968 she had become the first Black woman elected to Congress.

questions.question: In 1973, Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to fly past which planet?
questions.fact: It carries a small metal plaque with drawings of a man and a woman, in case anyone ever finds it.

questions.question: In 1974, Ella Grasso of Connecticut became the first woman to be elected governor without following whom?
questions.fact: Earlier women governors had followed their husbands into office.

questions.question: In November 1965, a huge power failure left about 30 million people in the dark in which part of the country?
questions.fact: In New York City, the lights went out at rush hour, but the night stayed surprisingly calm.

questions.question: Who was on the cover of the very first issue of People magazine, in March 1974?
questions.fact: She was starring in 'The Great Gatsby' at the time.

questions.question: Which preschool program for children from low-income families began in 1965?
questions.fact: It began as an eight-week summer program and soon became year-round.

questions.question: In 1971, an American team visited China to play which game, in what was called a sign of friendship?
questions.fact: It became known as 'ping-pong diplomacy,' and opened the way for President Nixon's 1972 trip.

questions.question: In October 1968, which Apollo mission sent the first live TV broadcast from an American spacecraft?
questions.fact: The crew held up cards for viewers, joking, "Keep those cards and letters coming in, folks!"

questions.question: Which daring fashion swept 1965, raising hemlines high above the knee?
questions.fact: It was a symbol of 'Swinging London,' where fashion designers turned it into a craze.

questions.question: In 'A Charlie Brown Christmas' (1965), what kind of Christmas tree does Charlie Brown pick?
questions.fact: The other kids laugh at it, but Linus helps him see what Christmas is really about.

questions.question: On TV's 1966 'Batman,' what was Batman's famous car called?
questions.fact: It was built from a 1955 Lincoln Futura concept car, rebuilt by customizer George Barris.

questions.question: A 1960s hippie who called your new record 'groovy' thought it was what?
questions.fact: It came from jazz musicians who were 'in the groove' when they played just right.

questions.question: When friends shouted 'Right on!' in the early 1970s, what were they saying?
questions.fact: It was a way of cheering someone on, a bit like a verbal high five.

questions.question: The first cash machine in the US opened in 1969 at a bank in New York. What does ATM stand for?
questions.fact: It was at a Chemical Bank branch in Rockville Centre, on Long Island.

questions.question: Walt Disney World opened in October 1971 near which Florida city?
questions.fact: Its first park was the Magic Kingdom, built on land many times larger than California's Disneyland.

questions.question: The 1970s leisure suit was usually made from which wrinkle-free fabric?
questions.fact: They often came in colors like powder blue, brown and pale green, with wide collars.

questions.question: Atari's 1972 arcade game 'Pong' was a simple video version of which sport?
questions.fact: It was one of the first video games to become a big hit.

questions.question: In Tony Orlando and Dawn's 1973 hit, what was tied 'round the old oak tree?
questions.fact: It was the year's top song in America. The ribbon was a sign that someone was welcome home.

questions.question: In 1974, daredevil Evel Knievel tried to jump across which canyon on a rocket cycle?
questions.fact: His parachute opened too early, and he floated down safely into the canyon.

questions.question: Which British designer is often credited with making the miniskirt a fashion hit?
questions.fact: Her shop, Bazaar, was on the King's Road in London.

questions.question: In mid-1960s slang, what did it mean to be 'with it'?
options: To be up to date and hip
questions.fact: Its opposite was being 'square.'

questions.question: The 1970s saying 'Keep on truckin'' came from the cartoons of which artist?
questions.fact: His strutting cartoon men showed up on T-shirts, posters and belt buckles everywhere.

questions.question: Bell-bottom pants were all the rage in the early 1970s. Where did the style come from?
questions.fact: Sailors could roll the wide legs up easily when they scrubbed the decks.

questions.question: During the 1973–74 gas shortage, many states let you buy gas only on certain days, based on what?
questions.fact: Plates ending in an odd number could fill up on odd-numbered days, and even numbers on even days.

questions.question: Which stackable potato chips, invented by Procter & Gamble in 1968, come in a tall round can?
questions.fact: Each chip is shaped like a saddle, so they stack neatly in the can without breaking.

questions.question: The Big Mac went on sale across the country in 1968. Who invented it?
questions.fact: Jim Delligatti created it at his restaurant near Pittsburgh in 1967.

questions.question: The peace sign seen at 1960s rallies was first designed in 1958 for a British campaign against what?
questions.fact: Designer Gerald Holtom combined the flag-signal letters N and D, for 'nuclear disarmament.'

questions.question: Which guitarist was the last act to play at Woodstock, on the Monday morning in 1969?
questions.fact: Rain delays pushed him to 8:30 a.m. By then the crowd had shrunk from about 450,000 to about 30,000.

questions.question: Which 1966 party game had players twisting to put their hands and feet on colored dots?
questions.fact: Sales took off after Johnny Carson played it with Eva Gabor on 'The Tonight Show.'

questions.question: Which tiny die-cast toy cars did Mattel launch in 1968?
questions.fact: They had low-friction wheels that made them much faster on their orange plastic tracks.

questions.question: Which soft foam ball, sold from 1969, was advertised as safe to throw indoors?
questions.fact: Ads said you could throw it in the house without breaking lamps or hurting babies.

questions.question: Which simple yellow design with a big grin became a huge fad around 1971?
questions.fact: It turned up on buttons, T-shirts and coffee mugs, often with the words 'Have a nice day.'

questions.question: Which sports drink was invented in 1965 for the University of Florida's football team?
questions.fact: It was named after the team, the Florida Gators.

questions.question: Which egg-shaped toys of the 1970s 'wobble, but they don't fall down'?
questions.fact: Hasbro's Playskool brand made them, and the weight in the bottom always set them upright again.

questions.question: What kind of bed, filled with water, became a big fad in the early 1970s?
questions.fact: A design student in San Francisco created the modern version in 1968.

questions.question: Which groovy lamp, sold in America from 1965, had blobs of wax rising and falling?
questions.fact: Its British inventor, Edward Craven Walker, first called it the 'Astro Lamp.'

questions.question: Which shiny white boots were the rage with miniskirts in the mid-1960s?
questions.fact: French designer André Courrèges helped make them famous in 1964.

questions.question: Which hamburger chain did Dave Thomas start in 1969, naming it after his daughter?
questions.fact: The first one opened in Columbus, Ohio, and served square hamburger patties.

questions.question: Which slow-cooker brand became a kitchen hit after it came out in 1971?
questions.fact: It began as a bean cooker called the Naxon Beanery before Rival bought it and renamed it.

questions.question: Which boxed mix, launched in 1971, turned a pound of ground beef into a whole meal?
questions.fact: Its mascot is a friendly white glove with a face, called the Helping Hand.

questions.question: Which low-riding plastic tricycle, sold from 1969, let kids race around with a giant front wheel?
questions.fact: It was made by the Louis Marx toy company, and kids loved how loud it rumbled on the sidewalk.

questions.question: Which coffee company opened its very first store at Seattle's Pike Place Market in 1971?
questions.fact: It was named after the first mate in the novel 'Moby-Dick.'

questions.question: Which fantasy role-playing game, played with dice and imagination, was first published in 1974?
questions.fact: Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson created it in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin.

questions.question: Which 1972 machine was the first video game system you could hook up to a home TV?
questions.fact: It came with plastic overlays to stick on the TV screen to make game boards.

questions.question: In 1973, Martin Cooper of Motorola made the first public call on what?
questions.fact: He made the call on a New York City street, and the phone weighed about 2.5 pounds.

questions.question: In 1974, the first item ever scanned by a barcode at a supermarket was a pack of what?
questions.fact: It happened at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio. That pack of gum is now in the Smithsonian.

questions.question: Which Chevrolet sports car was launched in 1966 to compete with Ford's Mustang?
questions.fact: Asked what a Camaro was, Chevrolet joked that it was 'a small, vicious animal that eats Mustangs.'

questions.question: Which bank charge card, started in 1966, was later renamed MasterCard?
questions.fact: A group of California banks created it to compete with BankAmericard.

questions.question: Which women's magazine, co-founded by Gloria Steinem, put out its first regular issue in 1972?
questions.fact: Its name used the new title 'Ms.,' which didn't depend on whether a woman was married.

questions.question: Which whipped topping in a plastic tub did Birds Eye introduce in 1966?
questions.fact: Within two years it was the best-selling item in Birds Eye's frozen food line.

questions.question: Which coating mix, launched in 1965, had families shaking chicken in a bag?
questions.fact: The TV ads featured a child saying, 'And I helped!'

questions.question: Which super-bouncy rubber ball did Wham-O release in 1965?
questions.fact: It could bounce almost as high as the spot it was dropped from. The Super Bowl name was partly inspired by it.

questions.question: Which 1967 toy let children make glowing pictures by pushing colored pegs into a light box?
questions.fact: Its jingle sang about 'making things with light.'

questions.question: Which tortilla chip brand, first sold at Disneyland, went on sale nationwide in 1966?
questions.fact: The chips were first made at a Mexican restaurant called Casa de Fritos inside the park.

questions.question: Which Texas airline, famous for low fares and cheerful flight attendants, began flying in 1971?
questions.fact: It started with just three planes flying between Dallas, Houston and San Antonio.

questions.question: Which tape format, offered in Ford cars starting in 1966, played music in an endless loop?
questions.fact: It was developed by Bill Lear, who also built the Learjet.

questions.question: Which company began overnight package delivery by air in 1973, with 14 small jets?
questions.fact: Founder Fred Smith based the company in Memphis, Tennessee.

questions.question: Which holiday, running from December 26 to January 1, was first celebrated in 1966?
questions.fact: Maulana Karenga created it to celebrate African American culture and family.
